children: By Deborah Acosta, Douglas Belkin, Jenny Strasburg and Juliet Chung

Ken Griffin has been talking to elite universities about his vision to remake the city of Miami for the last several years. He wanted to turn his new home into a global business hub, and to make that happen, South Florida needed a top technology school.
The universities of Oxford and Cambridge, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, and Vanderbilt University were among the institutions with which he held discussions.

In September, the Citadel chief executive announced that he would invest $2 billion in a partnership with Carnegie Mellon University to build a brand-new Miami campus. Another $1 billion would go to CMU's main campus in Pittsburgh.
A CMU press release referred to the combined $3 billion investment as the largest individual gift in higher education history.

The gift was striking not just for its size: Griffin is not an alumnus of the school. He has donated to other academic institutions, including at least half a billion dollars to his alma mater Harvard, but this project has ambition to help reshape a city.

"We regularly engage with leading universities, but the vision and model we developed with Carnegie Mellon over two years was unique," said a Citadel spokesman in a statement, citing the school's strength in computing and robotics among other attributes.
The scale of the investment reflects the big changes sweeping through higher education.

Elite academic institutions are weighing distant satellite campuses and unconventional partnerships as they grapple with shrinking student demographics, slower tuition growth, and the soaring costs of expanding AI and technology programs.
It also reflects significant changes in Miami.

In a few short years, thanks in part to a low-tax, pro-business environment, the city has become a magnet for some of the most powerful people in America, who are putting down roots in hopes that Miami could one day go toe-to-toe with Wall Street and Silicon Valley.

Griffin has had an outsize role in this transformation. He announced in 2022 that he would move the headquarters of Citadel, the hedge-fund firm he founded, and his market-making firm Citadel Securities, to Miami from Chicago. His plans include a 52-story Citadel headquarters as well as other major office and residential real estate acquisitions.

Griffin meets regularly with leaders of top schools about topics including expanding access to higher education and has made significant donations to several. His discussions with the universities about a Miami campus were wide ranging and the level of detail varied.

Griffin approached leadership at MIT with his vision for a Miami campus within the past four years, people familiar with the matter said. While the university has helped Singapore and Russia establish their own universities — Singapore University of Technology and Design and the Skolkovo Institute of Science and Technology in Moscow — it generally avoids creating satellite campuses, which are viewed by some administrators as logistical and administrative headaches. Nothing came of the talks.

Griffin also had discussions in 2024 with top administrators at the University of Oxford in the U.K. to discuss the possibility of an Oxford campus in Miami that would include his financial support, according to people familiar with the talks. Some Oxford officials expressed enthusiasm about pursuing a potential agreement with Griffin but ran into opposition from other officials, the people say.
Griffin also had some preliminary conversations with Cambridge about a new university, but they stopped short of formal proposals, a person familiar with the conversations said.
Officials at Vanderbilt University met with Griffin as that university explored plans for an expansion that has led to Vanderbilt outposts in four cities including New York and San Francisco.

Instead of Miami, Vanderbilt ultimately went to West Palm Beach. An alumnus, Cody Crowell, had recognized the opportunity for Vanderbilt and brought it up with Chancellor Daniel Diermeier at a football game in 2023.
The school worked with real-estate moguls Stephen Ross and Jeff Greene to acquire land in West Palm Beach for a Florida campus.
Griffin's conversations with CMU started about two years ago.

The new campus will be built on 35-acres in Miami's Wynwood neighborhood. About $1.1 billion was used to buy part of the site, which was owned by local real-estate developer Moishe Mana. Mana also helped Griffin's team acquire additional properties in the neighborhood for the campus.

Some $900 million will go toward building a campus. According to the announcement of the partnership, development plans include space for industry research labs and venture studios so students, faculty, industry and community partners can work alongside one another. The school will support more than 3,500 undergraduate, master's and Ph.D. students, nearly 300 faculty and over 600 staff members.
Construction is slated to begin in 2027, with the first students expected to enroll in 2028.
Griffin's multiyear effort underscores how complicated big donations can be for schools.

Even as universities are under greater financial stress than ever, the sector is consolidating and many research universities are eager to expand. Presidents routinely spend half of their time soliciting major donations, often to support expansion goals.

But there are risks to these kinds of gifts: They can take years to land and come with expectations, implicit or laid out in the black-and-white of a gift agreement. Poorly aligned interests can cause indigestion to institutions that prioritize their academic and operational autonomy.

University presidents are often hired for their fundraising prowess and judged on the projects they build. Trustees often have relationships with donors and are also eager to land big gifts. Turning down one prospective donor risks turning off the next donor who may be considering a gift of their own.
And even billionaire-funded projects that are unrestricted can generate unforeseen expenses and cost overruns.
"Development officers have a phrase for these potential donations: gifts that eat," said Ben Porter, founder of Principal Gift Strategies, a fundraising consulting firm.

For CMU President Farnam Jahanian, a Miami outpost offers a strategic expansion into a growing tech ecosystem at the ground floor, and a base from which to recruit elite Latin American engineering talent.

CMU is ranked highly in disciplines Griffin is interested in — computer science, artificial intelligence, robotics and quantitative finance — and for decades Citadel has tapped CMU as a prime recruiting pipeline for software engineers and quantitative analysts. In 2015 the university named a computer science lab and study space the Citadel Teaching Commons after Citadel donated money and equipment.
Though the CMU board of trustees voted unanimously to open the satellite campus in Miami, it took a prolonged negotiation by Griffin to get to an agreement with the school.

Griffin joined the board of trustees as part of the investment, and Paul Darrah, Citadel's chief workplace officer, is currently helping to manage the development project. CMU said it would soon be hiring a development officer and that the school would be "responsible for building the campus, setting the academic standards, recruiting faculty and advancing the educational and research mission of CMU Miami."

It could not be learned how the land ownership will be structured. To secure the 30-plus acres in Miami, Griffin tapped Citadel executives — including Gerald Beeson, Citadel's COO, and Cason Carter, Citadel's head of public affairs — to work with local partners to present Mana with a deal.

By the end of October, Gov. Ron DeSantis nominated the area in and around the campus as an Opportunity Zone, a federal tax designation that allows investors to defer and sometimes avoid taxes when they plow capital gains into real estate and other businesses located within it.
A few weeks earlier, on Oct. 1, DeSantis was in attendance at the announcement party in Miami for the CMU campus, as were local mayors, Citadel executives, and CMU administrators and trustees.

The invitation-only crowd mingled in a Wynwood warehouse decorated by lush potted palms. One CMU trustee expressed anxiety about a possible uphill battle for the school as it works to raise the rest of the funds it will need to make the campus successful.
Griffin walked into the party out of a torrential downpour, stepping out from under an umbrella as he put on his suit jacket. "It's like rain on your wedding day," he quipped.
